kernels.definition: A UX research plan turns a decision need into actionable learning objectives, participants, tasks, evidence-capture roles, and a rehearsal-ready study setup.

definitionAnchor.quote: Each round of user research should have clear objectives. Keep your objectives actionable and to the point.

facts.text: The team should agree what it wants to learn from the research round before selecting study details.

anchor.quote: Work with your team to agree what you want to learn from a round of research.

facts.text: A prototype used in research should work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue.

anchor.quote: Your prototype or beta service needs to work from end-to-end and be usable and accessible from the research venue.

facts.text: Researchers should run through test tasks on the day before the research session.

anchor.quote: Run through the test tasks on the day before the research.

facts.text: A practice session with a team member can expose procedure problems before participants arrive.

anchor.quote: To make sure your research goes smoothly, consider running through the session with a team member.

kernels.definition: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.

definitionAnchor.quote: user profiles or personas that describe groups of users with similar behaviour and needs

facts.text: Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.

anchor.quote: Present what you've learned in a way that's easy for others to understand and share.

facts.text: User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.

anchor.quote: User needs tend to be high-level, broad in scope and stable over time.

facts.text: Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.

anchor.quote: These describe the specific features and content you need to create for your service to meet your users' needs.

facts.text: Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

anchor.quote: This traceability allows you to track related activities and determine how well you're meeting a particular user need.

kernels.definition: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.

definitionAnchor.quote: It's important for teams to make sure the thing they're building forms a coherent part of a user's wider journey.

facts.text: A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.

anchor.quote: Start by talking to your users to learn more about the steps they have to take and the transactions involved.

facts.text: An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.

anchor.quote: The map should show which bits of the journey users are struggling with and the areas you might want to focus on improving.

facts.text: A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.

anchor.quote: dead ends in the user journey

facts.text: Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

anchor.quote: online and offline elements of the transaction not joining up in an intuitive way

kernels.definition: A task flow analysis diagrams the steps and decision points through which a user interacts with a system to reach a defined goal.

definitionAnchor.quote: A task flow analysis is a step-by-step diagram showing how a user interacts with a system to reach a goal.

facts.text: Task flow analysis can validate the team's understanding of user goals, common scenarios, and tasks.

anchor.quote: Validate your understanding of users' goals, common scenarios, and tasks

facts.text: A task flow should show how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.

anchor.quote: Illustrate the overall flow of tasks through which a user progresses to accomplish a goal

facts.text: Task flow analysis should surface obstacles that stand between users and their goals.

anchor.quote: Surface obstacles in the way of users achieving their goal

facts.text: The diagram may include multiple possible paths, task sequences, and decision points.

anchor.quote: The diagram traces a user's possible paths through sequences of tasks and decision points to meet their goal.

kernels.definition: Interactive prototyping builds a testable representation of how a planned experience looks and works without requiring every production detail.

definitionAnchor.quote: A prototype is an interactive (high-fidelity) version of the experience you are planning to build. It shows how the design will look and work, without full detail.

facts.text: Prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works.

anchor.quote: Combined with other methods like usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough, prototypes help you test whether a design concept will work.

facts.text: Functional prototypes allow a team to observe how users interact with a product.

anchor.quote: Functional prototypes help you observe how users interact with the product.

facts.text: A prototype should show the major interactions even when not every interaction is functional.

anchor.quote: Show the major interactions. Not all interactions need to be functional.

facts.text: Prototypes should support fast iteration and be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.

anchor.quote: Iterate. Prototypes should be quick to create and even quicker to discard.

kernels.definition: Accessibility and usability evaluation combines standards-based conformance checks with observation of representative users completing realistic tasks.

definitionAnchor.quote: WCAG 2.2 is designed to apply broadly to different web technologies now and in the future, and to be testable with a combination of automated testing and human evaluation.

facts.text: WCAG organizes web accessibility around the principles perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust.

anchor.quote: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust

facts.text: Evaluation with disabled and older users can find barriers that conformance evaluation alone does not reveal.

anchor.quote: Evaluating with users with disabilities and with older users identifies usability issues that are not discovered by conformance evaluation alone.

facts.text: A usability test observes users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.

anchor.quote: A usability test observes users as they attempt to use a product or service while thinking out loud.

facts.text: A single disabled participant's experience should not be generalized to all people with disabilities.

anchor.quote: Avoid assuming that input from one person with a disability applies to all people with disabilities.

mcItems.q: What should the team establish prior to selecting study details?
op: The specific evidence capture roles
The desired learning objectives
The rehearsal-ready study setup
The specific tasks
mcItems.ex: Selecting study details should follow agreement on what the team wants to learn from the research round. Choosing the specific tasks is premature before defining the learning goals.

mcItems.q: What condition must a prototype meet for use in a research venue?
op: It must be fully accessible
It must be usable and accessible
It must work end-to-end
It must be rehearsed beforehand
mcItems.ex: A prototype used in research must work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue. Simply being accessible is insufficient if the prototype fails to function.

mcItems.q: Which characteristic is essential for a prototype when aiming to support rapid iteration?
op: It must require every production detail.
It should be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.
It must show every interaction perfectly.
It should only focus on functional interactions.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that prototypes should be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them (Claim 4). The misconception is that prototypes must require every production detail (Claim 0).

mcItems.q: How can prototypes be effectively utilized to validate a design concept?
op: By requiring every production detail for testing.
By combining them with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough.
By only showing fully functional interactions.
By ensuring every interaction is perfectly functional.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works (Claim 1). The misconception is that prototypes must only show fully functional interactions (Claim 2).

mcItems.q: Which characteristic is essential for a prototype when aiming to support rapid iteration?
op: It must require every production detail.
It should be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.
It must show every interaction perfectly.
It should only focus on functional interactions.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that prototypes should be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them (Claim 4). The misconception is that prototypes must require every production detail (Claim 0).

mcItems.q: How can prototypes be effectively utilized to validate a design concept?
op: By requiring every production detail for testing.
By combining them with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough.
By only showing fully functional interactions.
By ensuring every interaction is perfectly functional.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works (Claim 1). The misconception is that prototypes must only show fully functional interactions (Claim 2).
